comments.author: theonemind
comments.story_title: Ask HN: When did tech stop being cool?
comments.why_zh: 论证软件正处于衰败时代，正在失去基础。
comments.quote_zh: 我认为 Jonathan Blow 提出了一个不错的论点：我们正处于软件的衰败时代。
comments.text_zh: [VIDEO] 我认为 Jonathan Blow 提出了一个不错的论点：我们正处于软件的衰败时代。在衰败时代，文明仍然在做、也仍然能做那件事，但已经开始失去对基础原理的把握，所以它正在走向衰落。衰败时代是一种终结，但未必感觉像终结，更像是停滞地瞎折腾。你认识多少能写汇编代码的程序员？一个 web 应用和硅片之间有多少层抽象？处理器、操作系统，可能还有字节码 VM，可能还有框架……一路都在一点点漏。他说得很有道理——我们能写出好软件的证据在哪里？看起来有可能，但它并没有出现，所以说到底，那种也许我们能行的感觉只是一种感觉，不是证据。
comments.text: [VIDEO] I think Jonathan Blow made a decent argument that we're in a decadent age of software. In a decadent age, the civilization still does and can do the thing, but has started to lose a grip on the fundamentals, so it's on the way out. A decadent age is a kind of end, doesn't necessarily feel like the end, it kind of feels like a stagnant bumbling. How many programmers do you know that can write assembly code? How many layers of abstraction between a web app and the silicon? Processor, OS, probably a byte-code VM, probably a framework... leaking a little bit all of the way. He makes a good point--where's the evidence that we can write good software? It seems possible , but it doesn't appear, so really, the feeling that maybe we could is just a feeling, not evidence.

comments.text_zh: “社会中最优的欺诈数量是 0”——你确定吗？为什么？Bad Things(tm) 对测试和改进安全性/安防是有用的，而当我看到那些对 Bad Things(tm) 毫无应对经验的个人/机构时，我就知道，等坏事真的发生，他们要吃大苦头。也许你的意思是，那些不被起诉的……或没被发现的欺诈的最优数量……？即便是那样，我也要主张，有一小部分是有用的，能让安全/安防行业保持警觉、随时待命。作为一个佐证：如果你相信战争（世界和平）并不是一个已解决的问题，那么你的城市/地区/文明/种族面临存亡威胁就只是时间问题，而唯一真正的准备就是随时准备创新和动员。如果这听起来很阴暗，抱歉。我的意思和“农民只占一小部分比例是可取的”是同一个道理。相比之下，我参观过斯德哥尔摩的一家传统丝绸工厂（顺便说一句，非常棒），那门手艺已经失传到他们很难找到能操作织布机和其他老设备的工匠的地步。参见 Jonathan Blow 关于失传技术的精彩演讲：[VIDEO]
comments.text: "optimal amount of fraud in society is 0" - are you sure? why? Bad Things(tm) are useful for testing and improving safety/security, and when I see people/institutions with no experience reacting to Bad Things(tm), I know they're in for a world of hurt when it does happen. Perhaps you mean, the optimal amount of fraud that isn't prosecuted... or not detected... ? Even then, I'd argue that there's a tiny percentage that's useful for keeping the safety/security industry on its toes and at the ready. As a proof point, if you believe that war (world peace) is not a solved problem, then it's only a matter of time before your city/region/civilization/race faces an existential threat, for which the only true preparation is to be ready to innovate and mobilize. Sorry if this comes across as dark. I mean it in the same vein as having a small percentage of farmers is desirable. By contrast, I visited a traditional silk factory in Stockholm (amazing btw) and the craft has been lost to the point where they're struggling to find craftspeople able to work their looms and other old equipment. See Jonathan Blow's excellent talk about lost technology: [VIDEO]

comments.text_zh: 就在几天前，我还提到我经常看到龙书被当成出气筒。似乎不知从什么时候起，这本书连同 K&R 一起，成了毫无根据的批评的靶子。我追问过细节，也见过别人这么做，但最后从没落到任何具体东西上——只是含蓄地诉诸一种新的“常识”：它们弊大于利。这让我想起 Reddit 上的“真相”是怎么被合成出来的。这里有个反例：Russ Cox 有一系列关于正则表达式的文章，开篇是 Regular Expression Matching Can Be Simple And Fast < [LINK] >。在过去几年里，它广受好评。在文中，他为 Thompson NFAs 做了论证，也在一些地方惋惜这种方法没有更广为人知，已经成了一种失传的知识。（另见 Jonathan Blow 的 < [VIDEO] >。）不过，尽管对龙书有那么多批评，你大概会以为这意味着读过它的人足够多，总该有人指出 Thompson 在第 3 章被引用，而且他的方法在那里有相当详细的描述。我觉得实际情况是，就像 The Art Of Computer Programming 一样，龙书被广泛引用，却很少被真正阅读。现在，进入 21 世纪的迷因工厂。话虽如此，我最近看到的一条评论随口贬低龙书——讽刺的是，说它的“二流方法”“阻碍了”编译器发展——这确实促使我去翻那本 boo
comments.text: It was just a few days ago when I mentioned how often I see the dragon book held up as a punching bag. It seems that at some point the book, along with K&R, have become the target for unsubstantiated criticism. I've pressed for details, and I've seen others do the same, but it never ends in anything concrete—just an implicit appeal to the new conventional wisdom that they do more harm than good. Reminds me of how "truth" gets synthesized on Reddit. Here's a counterexample: Russ Cox has a series on regular expressions, beginning with Regular Expression Matching Can Be Simple And Fast < [LINK] >. In the last several years, it has become very well-received. In it, he lays out the case for Thompson NFAs, and also laments in some places about how the approach is not more widely known, having become a sort of lost knowledge. (See also Jonathan Blow's < [VIDEO] >.) For all the criticism of the dragon book, though, you'd think that would mean enough people have read it that someone would have pointed out that Thompson is cited in Chapter 3, where his approach is described in some detail. I think that what's actually going on is that, like The Art Of Computer Programming, the dragon book is widely referenced and rarely read. Now, enter the 21st century meme factory. Having said that, the most recent comment I saw that was being casually dismissive of the dragon book—ironically for its "second-rate methods" that have "held back" compiler development—did motivate me into digging the boo

comments.story_title: There Is No Software Maintenance
comments.text_zh: 在我工作过的所有公司里，我与软件维护的关系都令人非常沮丧。我一直非常、非常坚信这样一个类比：你估计核工程师花多少时间在运行和维护现有反应堆上，又有多少时间在建造新反应堆上？公共公路部门呢，新建道路 vs 修复或改善现有道路？没有哪个类比是完美的，但我能得出的唯一合乎逻辑的结论是：相对于几乎所有“我们造的东西要用好多年”的同行学科，软件工程是一门非常奇怪的学科。它奇怪，是因为在我经历过的组织中，我们长期在维护上投入不足，然后当新开发项目赶不上截止日期或拖个没完时又表现得手忙脚乱；但它也奇怪，因为我所有的经验都在冲我大喊：“我甚至不确定我们是否知道怎么把系统维护好。”我在一家组织（一家你肯定听说过的上市公司）见过这种情况：多年前我们有过并且达成过“99.999% 可用性”这样的宏大目标；而今天，整个 API 范围内能到三个九就是好月份了。在和非常资深、聪明的工程师开团队会议时，当我们问“我们该怎么改进”，你会开始观察到那种习得性无助——他们提的都是些小改动，比如，你知道的，给某个外部 API 加个缓存，或者把内置的 HTTP 客户端换成另一个超时参数更齐全的，诸如此类。我和他们私下聊，说：这是真的
comments.text: I have had a really frustrating relationship with software maintenance in all of the companies I've worked for. I've always been a strong, strong believer in an analogy like: How much time would you estimate that nuclear engineers spend operating and maintaining existing reactors, versus building new ones? How about public highway departments and building new roads, versus fixing or improving existing ones? No analogy is ever perfect, but the only logical conclusion I can reach is that software engineering is a really weird discipline relative to practically all of its "we build things that last years" peers. Its weird because, well, our organizations in my experience chronically under-invest in maintenance then act flustered when new developments don't meet deadlines or take forever; but its also weird because all of my experience screams at me "I'm not even sure if we know how to maintain systems well". I've seen this in one org (a public company you'd recognize); where years ago we had and met lofty goals like "99.999% availability"; today its a good month if we hit three-nines, API wide. In team meetings with really senior, smart engineers when we ask How Can We Improve This, you start observing this learned helplessness where they suggest small changes like, you know, adding a cache for some external API, or replacing the built-in HTTP client with some other one that has a more comprehensive knob for timeouts, or whatever. I talk with them privately and say: Is this real
